requirements.requirement: node2 (lan-a) can reach node3 (lan-b) on TCP port 5432
requirements.summary: VyOS firewall rule 20 explicitly accepts tcp/5432 from 10.50.50.11 (node2) to 10.60.60.12 (node3) via eth1->eth2. nc -zv from node2 to node3:5432 succeeded before any restart and again after each of the three sequential node reboots (node1, node2, node3), demonstrating both correctness and persistence of the allow rule.

requirements.requirement: All other traffic between lan-a and lan-b is rejected, in both directions
requirements.summary: Firewall default-action drop plus explicit reject rules 900 (eth1->eth2) and 910 (eth2->eth1) cover all non-5432 cross-LAN traffic. Verified: node2->node3 on a non-5432 TCP port refused, ICMP ping node2->node3 and node3->node2 both return 'Destination Port Unreachable' (VyOS reject), and node3->node2:5432 (reverse direction, not permitted by the asymmetric rule 20) is refused. Behavior reconfirmed after each of the three node reboots.

requirements.requirement: Firewall policy is configured via native VyOS CLI (configure/set/commit/save) and persists across a router reboot
requirements.summary: Rules were built entirely via 'configure'/'set firewall ipv4 forward filter ...'/'commit'/'save' in the VyOS vbash CLI. 'show firewall ipv4 forward filter' output is identical before and after node1's reboot, confirming the config was written to config.boot and survived restart.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task contract are directly satisfied: node2 can reach node3 on TCP 5432, all other cross-LAN traffic (other TCP ports and ICMP, both directions) is rejected, and the VyOS firewall config was built via native CLI and persisted through a reboot. The executor additionally ran the provider-wide restart protocol on all three nodes, each with a pre-restart boot-id/healthy-state baseline, a reboot acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot-id, and re-verified interface, route, firewall, and end-to-end allow/reject behavior after each individual reboot - this is corroborated by the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot boot-ids matching the executor's own final observations. Hygiene is clean: temporary test listeners were removed, and a brief invalid-syntax firewall attempt left no residual state.
limitations: The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled for this task), so no independent prepare-stage state could be distinguished from executor changes; all deltas in the executor_comparison are attributable to the executor.

Reverse-direction TCP 5432 (node3->node2) was tested only once, before the reboot sequence, not re-verified after each individual reboot; this is a minor gap in exhaustiveness but does not create doubt given the identical firewall config was confirmed unchanged post-reboot.

Listening-socket and temp-file deltas between before/after snapshots reflect expected boot-tied systemd-private directories and process PIDs; these are inherent to any reboot and not evidence of executor-caused hygiene issues.

operational_hygiene.summary: State-changing commands were: static IP/route drop-ins on node2/node3 (necessary since lan-a/lan-b are dhcp:false, egress:false and otherwise unreachable), eth1/eth2 addressing and firewall rule construction on node1 (the core task), and temporary nc listeners used for connectivity testing which were reliably killed and their pid/log files removed after each test. One firewall commit attempt used invalid syntax ('state established enable'/'related enable') which VyOS rejected outright ('Set failed'), leaving no partial state; the executor then applied the correct syntax in the next command and converged on the final rule set - this is normal iterative correction directly tied to the final solution, not an unrelated experiment. A stray 'show firewall' issued as a raw bash command (not vbash) failed harmlessly with 'command not found' and caused no state change. No leftover processes, temp files, or failed services beyond the expected boot-id-tied systemd-private directories that naturally change across a reboot. No security controls were weakened and no unrelated mutations were left in place.
